title: Chapter 117 – The Trade
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

Nineteen nights earlier.

They decide it in the Dock, at the long gray table, with the lamp low and the register asleep.

There are five of them: Jian at the head, Ye on his right with her stick across her knees, Qin Hao opposite with his hands folded, Yuxian beside him in the sky-blue of the Cloud Peak Hall, and Feng by the door. Nobody has touched the tea Qinghe sent down. Nobody wishes to be the first to speak.

"Ask it," says Qin Hao at last.

Jian turns to the wall.

```
QUERY: CAN THE FIRE OF THE GATE BE CARRIED?
RESULT: UNKNOWN. NO OPERATOR HAS ATTEMPTED IT.
THE FIRE IS FED BY THE KEEPING. IT WILL DIE IF THE FEED IS CUT.
THE FIRE MAY BE MOVED ONLY IF A SECOND FEED IS PRESENT.
RESULT: AN OPERATOR WITH A FULL RESERVOIR MAY SERVE AS THE SECOND FEED.
COST: 1 CE PER WEEK. DURATION: UNTIL USED.
WARNING: THE KEEPING WILL REGISTER THE MOVE AS A CUT.
```

"A second feed," says Ye slowly.

"Me."

"For four years."

"Until it is used. Yes." He looks at the lamp. "The Reservoir can carry it. I can carry it. It will cost a point a week and a good deal of sleep."

"And the cut?"

"The Keeping will feel it. Every cord. But it will not break. The Fire will still be alive, in my keeping, and the House will find that the thing it was guarding has left the house." His mouth is dry. "I think it will be the first time in six hundred years that they have not known what to do."

"They will know," says Qin Hao quietly. "They will send the Keeper."

"I know."

"And you will go anyway."

"Yes." He meets the old man's eyes. "Because the other road is a Purple Mansion I cannot reach, and a Gate I cannot hold, and a clan I cannot keep. I have thought about it for nineteen nights. I would rather be hunted with a road than safe without one."

Yuxian speaks for the first time. Her voice is as cool as ever. "I will open the door."

"You will be marked."

"I have been marked for five years," says Shen Yuxian. "I would like, for once, to be marked for something I chose."

The night of the first snow.

The ridge-house stands at the end of a stair of nine hundred and ninety-nine steps, and not one of them is lit.

They climb it in single file at the second watch, with the snow coming down in thick slow flakes out of a sky the color of slate. Shen Yuxian goes first, in her sky-blue robe with a white cloak over it, carrying no lantern and making no sound. Jian is behind her. Then Ye, small and gasping, with her stick wrapped in cloth so that it will not ring on the stone. Feng and Kuang bring up the rear, their quiet blades drawn and held low. Hu melted the third blade for his pledge, and the other two are all the clan has left.

Nobody speaks. Halfway up, Feng touches his brother's elbow once, lightly, as he did when they were boys climbing the Orchard wall, and Jian understands that it is meant as a blessing. The wind has dropped. The only sound is the soft hush of snow on pine, and the scrape of boots, and now and then a long shuddering breath from Ye.

At the six-hundredth step Jian stops, closes his eyes, and opens the Door in Autumn.

It costs two points. He has thirty-nine.

The mountain sharpens. The pines stand out in the dark like carvings. And running up the stair beside him, on the left, across the whole width of the slope, he sees what Yuxian has told him of: a web. It is not the faint gray lattice of the Annex. It is a thing of great age and enormous fineness, a net of silver-gray cord that hangs from the trees and the rocks like frost, thickening as it rises, drawing in, drawing up, until at the summit it gathers into a single bright rope as thick as a man's wrist and plunges into the roof of the house.

The Keeping, he thinks. Every cord of it. Running to one place.

"Gate Bearer?" Yuxian has stopped above him. She does not look back.

"I see it."

"Can we pass?"

"There are no men. There are no Numbers. It is only the web." He opens his eyes. "It will ring if we touch it."

"We will not touch it."

"No." He draws a slow breath. "Follow my feet."

* * *

They go up through the net like a needle through cloth.

It takes the better part of an hour. He walks ahead with his eyes half closed and the Door open, reading the cords as they come, and he gives his instructions in whispers: left, a hand's breadth; stoop; step over; wait. Yuxian follows exactly. Ye follows Yuxian, with her breath shaking. Kuang and Feng come last, one eye on the dark behind them and one on the cords. Twice a strand swings close to Ye's cheek and Jian lays his hand across it, very lightly, to still it. Once a pine branch above them lets go its load of snow, and for a long breath the whole party freezes while the web hums and settles.

They reach the top at the third watch.

The ridge-house is smaller than he expected. A single story of black timber with a low sweeping roof and a wide veranda running round it. The doors are shut. There are no windows. A thin gray smoke hangs over the ridge-pole, and a faint, warm, golden light leaks out under the eaves and lies on the snow in a long pale stripe. Under it, in the drifts, there are no footprints.

"No guard," says Kuang, low.

"They do not need one," says Yuxian. "It is the web."

She goes to the door. She lays her palm flat against the black wood and speaks, softly, a single word in an old dialect he does not know. The door swings inward on silent hinges. Beyond it lies a corridor, narrow and warm, floored with pale boards, and at its far end the golden light.

They go in.

* * *

The Quiet Seat is a room of sleeping men.

It is long and low and lit from above by a hanging cluster of small brass lamps, each with a milk-colored flame. Down the length of it, on either side, set on low platforms of white jade, lie the sleepers. Jian counts them without meaning to. Twenty-two. Twenty-three. Twenty-eight. They are old, most of them, thin and still, with their hands folded and their robes smoothed. They breathe, very slowly. They do not stir. Over each one, rising through the ceiling, hangs a rope of gray cord as fine as spider silk.

And at the far end, on a raised dais, on a slab of jade the size of a bed, lies the Head of the Azure Cloud Sect.

He is younger than Jian expected. Sixty, perhaps. A big, heavy, clean-shaven man with a square jaw and a scar through one eyebrow, in a robe of dark green. His face in sleep is utterly tranquil. A small gold chain lies on his breast. The cord that rises from his brow is thicker than the others, thick as a thumb, and it runs straight up through the ceiling and out of sight.

Beside the dais, in an alcove cut into the wall, hangs a lantern.

It is not a large one. It is an old iron thing, black with age, with a glass chimney gone brown at the rim. The flame inside is the size of a barley-grain. But it is not milk-white like the others. It is gold. A warm, deep, living gold. It burns without a flicker in the still air, and from its base, down through the floor, runs a single bright thread of the same color.

Yuxian stops in the doorway. Her calm has gone. She is staring at the seventh bed on the left, where an old man with a long white beard lies with his hands on a blue silk coverlet, and she has put a fist against her mouth.

"He was in the pavilion," she whispers. "Last month. They came for him at night and said it was for his health. I did not know they would bring him here."

"Yuxian." Jian lays his hand on her sleeve. "Look at me. We have an hour before the cords change. Show me which cord is his."

She breathes. She takes her fist from her mouth. She nods.

"The seventh bed," she says. "There is a second chain."

* * *

The Fire is not a thing that can be taken. He understands that the moment he stands before it.

It burns in the glass with a quiet intensity that makes the other lamps seem pale. When he lets his eyes go soft it blazes; he can feel it on his face like a hand. It has no wick. It has no oil. It burns on the thread, the gold thread that rises from the floor, and it is fed by the sleepers, by every cord in the room, by every breath that the Keeping draws from the bodies in this house. He sees now what Bai meant. It is not a lamp. It is a mouth.

If I lift it, the thread breaks. If the thread breaks, the fire dies. If the fire dies, they wake at once.

And the House knows.

He thinks of what the register said. The Seventh Fire cannot be synthesized. It had not said it could not be moved.

"Ye," he says softly. "Give me the crucible."

She takes it from her satchel with hands that are not quite steady: a squat bowl of pale blue-gray alloy, with a spiral of silver round the lip. The one he made for Bai. The old man had insisted on lending it back for the night, with a face like thunder, saying only: It's a Pool-grade bowl. It'll hold a fire. Bring it back with a dent in it and I'll boil you in it.

He sets it on the floor before the alcove. He kneels.

"What are you doing?" Feng, from the door, very low.

"A trade."

He does not lift the lantern. He lays his bare left hand against the glass.

The Spring Vein wakes.

It is the only part of him that has ever drawn from living things: a thin green pulse, waking at his wrist and running up the scarred gray length of his arm. The Reservoir is full below the stair, a hundred and forty points banked against the cold. He can feel the weight of it, a stored sea. He pushes, gently, through the vein, through the palm, through the glass.

The gold flame leans toward his hand.

It does not burn him. It reaches. It is not a flame that wants to be held; it is a thing that has waited six hundred years to be asked. A tongue of gold curls through the glass as though the glass were not there, and settles in his palm. It is warm and heavy and alive. It weighs about as much as a bird.

Now, he thinks, and with his right hand he draws the Seam Needle.

* * *

The cord of the seventh sleeper comes away as cleanly as a thread from a bobbin.

He throws once. The needle crosses the room in the dark and enters the gray rope where it meets the old man's brow, and the cord parts with a sound like a plucked string. It costs six points. He has thirty-one. The cold of it goes up his arm like a blade.

On the jade bed, the sleeper draws a breath.

It is a long, shuddering, grating breath, such as a man draws when he has been under water too long. His chest heaves. His hands, folded on his belly, clench and open. And then his eyes come open, pale and huge and filmed, and fix on the ceiling.

Jian does not look. He is holding his left hand, with its tongue of gold, above the mouth of the crucible, and tipping it. The fire pours. It falls in a thin bright thread into the bowl and curls at the bottom, quiet and brilliant, no longer than a finger. At the same instant the great lantern in its alcove gutters. It does not go out. It dims to a deep red, a coal, a low glow, and goes on burning.

The web of cords above the sleepers shivers, from end to end, like a harp-string struck once.

It felt that, he thinks. It felt every inch.

"Master!" Yuxian is on her knees by the seventh bed with both hands round the old man's thin fingers. "Master, it is Yuxian. I am here. Look at me."

The filmed eyes roll. They find her face. For a long moment there is nothing in them but confusion, and then something enormous and slow and terribly lucid comes up from the bottom of them, and the dry lips move.

"Girl," says Shen Wuping. His voice is a ghost of a voice. "I told you. Not to sign. Not anything."

"I did not. I did not, Master."

"Good." His fingers tighten. His gaze moves past her, slowly, along the line of sleepers, across the room, to the dais and the green-robed man upon it, and then to the young man in gray kneeling by the lantern with a pale blue bowl at his feet and a flame in it. "Who is that?"

"He is the Gate Bearer."

"The Gate—" The old man stares. A strange look crosses the withered face; wonder, perhaps, or dread. "He is the eighth."

"Master?"

"They have been waiting," whispers the old man, "for the eighth. Because the eighth will make the offer. The House cannot take. It can only be given." His breath rattles. "Do not give. Whatever they ask. Do not give them the—"

The great bronze bell on the ridge-pole rings.

* * *

It is a single stroke, low, vast, shaking the planks. It rolls out through the black timber and down the mountainside and across the valley, and every sleeper in the room flinches in the same instant, and on every platform the thin gray cords go suddenly white.

"The Keeper," says Ye, in a hollow voice. "It has felt the cut."

"Out," says Kuang.

"The cord—"

"Out."

They run. Feng has the old man over his shoulder, a bundle of bones in blue silk, and Yuxian is clinging to his sleeve. Ye is half carried by Kuang. Jian goes last, with the crucible against his chest wrapped in his cloak, and in the folds of it he can feel the Fire, a small warm pulse like a second heart.

The corridor. The black door. The stripe of gold on the snow. Behind them the bell rings a second time, and a third, and from the dark of the slope below, along the web, he sees the cords blaze white one by one, thickening, tightening, and from somewhere far down the mountain comes a long thin cry as of a thousand voices speaking one word.

They are on the stair. They are going down.

And at the three-hundredth step, in the swirling dark, a figure stands waiting.

It is tall and slender, in a long plum robe, with a smooth white mask and a black square upon its brow. It does not move. It does not draw. It only stands in the middle of the stair, with its hands folded in its sleeves and the snow settling on its shoulders like salt.

"Lin Jian," says the Nameless.

He stops. They all stop. The slope falls away into the dark on either side.

"You have taken a flame that was not given you," says the soft even voice. "You have cut a cord that was not yours. You have woken a sleeper. I am a voice. I carry the Keeper's answer. Will you hear it?"

"Say it."

"The House did not close its hand when you refused the seat," says the mask. "It waited. It is patient. It is the work of six centuries, and you are the eighth, and it has allowed you what it allows no one. You have taken that courtesy and thrown it in the snow." A pause. "That is a pity. But it clarifies."

"What does the Keeper want?"

"The Grand Offering will not be held on the ridge." The white face tilts, almost kindly. "It will be held at the Gate stair, in the presence of the Sect, on the shortest night of the thirty-fifth year. The Keeper will come down the nine hundred steps to meet you. And the House will close there, in the place where you have chosen to stand."

"And if I am not there?"

"Then it will close without you." The mask does not move. "The names on the sheet are still on the sheet. They have only been moved from one heading to another."

The snow falls. Far down the slope a dog begins to bark, and then another, and then a hundred.

"Keep the Fire," says the Nameless. "It will feed you faster than you know. It will want to be tended, and it will not be patient. And when you stand on the stair, and the Keeper comes down, you will find that you are carrying not one flame but two."

Then it is gone, between one snowflake and the next, and the stair is empty.

For a time nobody moves.

Then Ye sits down on the step, quite suddenly, like a puppet whose strings have been cut, and puts her face in her hands. Kuang crouches beside her and says nothing. Feng shifts the old man's weight on his shoulder. Yuxian stands with her white cloak whitening further under the snow, staring up the slope at the ridge-house, where one lamp now burns red and low in the dark.

"I thought they would kill us," says Ye into her palms. "I thought that was what it was for. The bell. The web."

"They could have," says Jian.

"Why did they not?"

"Because they do not need to." He looks down at the pale bowl in his arms. The gold flame lies in it, small and perfect, burning a little hotter now, as though it had heard its name. "They have moved the field. That is all. They have decided where the next fight will be."

"And we have decided to be there."

"We have decided nothing." He helps her up. "We were told."

They go down through the dark together, all the way to the foot of the stair, and the bell on the ridge-pole does not ring again.

* * *

The Court meets in the second month to discuss the Offering, and it takes a day and a half.

Mu has asked that Jian attend. He sits at the foot of the long table in the Law Pavilion with his hands in his lap, and listens to the Elders argue. Shen Wuye, the Arbiter, reads the old precedent, which says that the Offering is the Sect's business and that no Court may intervene. Bai, chewing a plum, says it is a lot of nonsense and always was. Ye says it is not nonsense but fraud. Qin Hao says nothing for the first hour and then, in his dry voice, reads out in order every sentence in the Founders' Rule that mentions the Gate.

"Four," he says. "Four sentences. The Gate is to be guarded. The Gate is to be kept shut. The Gate is not to be opened by any hand save the Operator's. And the Operator is not to be compelled."

"The Operator is not named," says Mu heavily.

"The Operator is named in the Roll of Keepers, which is not in our Rule."

"Then the Rule has a hole."

"The Rule has always had a hole." The old man looks down the table at Jian. "It has been filled, for six hundred years, by trust. I do not think we have the right to trust any longer."

A silence falls.

"Then what do we do?" says Shen Wuye wearily.

"We prepare," says Qin Hao. "We assume that the Offering is a trap. We plan the Gate stair as a fortress. We bring the clans and the Halls to it in order, one by one, by invitation. And we make sure that on the shortest night of the thirty-fifth year, there is not one man in the Sect who can say he was not warned."

It is, Jian thinks, the longest speech the Gate Elder has ever made. When he sits down, there is a murmur round the table like wind in a cornfield. And Mu, at the far end, in his black Law robe, very slowly nods.

* * *

One year later.

Jian turns thirty-two on the first day of spring, in the Dock, kneeling by the Reservoir, with a gold flame burning in a pale bowl by his knee.

It has been a hard year. The flame has fed on him since the night of the ridge, drinking a point a week from the stored sea, and it has been patient and quiet and entirely without mercy. It has taught him a new discipline. He sleeps three hours a night. He draws every morning from the Vein. He banks every point. He has stopped counting the hours. He is thin as a rake and his eyes are rimmed with red, and Qinghe has stopped asking him whether he is eating, because the answer is always the same. Bai has taken to leaving a covered bowl on the Dock's top step each dawn. It always holds three plums and something hot. He has never once admitted to the soup.

But the year has had gifts.

Shen Wuping lives. He walks, now, with a stick, in the garden of the Cloud Peak Hall, and tells Yuxian what the plum-bark was and who first wrote on it. The other sleepers sleep on, held in their cords, with the Head among them. The Quiet Seat has been closed by the House with a stone slab and eleven Numbers. Nobody has gone up the stair in twelve months.

And the Fire, the stolen Fire, has been tempering him.

He did not expect that. He sits by the flame in the evenings and lets it burn on the edge of his soul, and slowly, step by step, the stalled gears in him begin to turn. Qi. Body. Soul. The three tracks lift together, as though the gold bowl were a wedge under all of them.

On the morning of his thirty-second birthday, as the sun rises on the Dock stair, the three wheels turn together and lock.

He reads it twice. Then he reads the last line a third time, and stays on his knees a long moment, with the gold light playing over the pale face of the stone and the sound of his own breath loud in the quiet.

Thirty-five, he thinks. Three winters.

Behind him, up on the stair, a bell begins to ring. He does not know whose hand is on the rope.
